tagline: Elephants, diamonds, and a river that vanishes
overview:
Botswana is a landlocked country in southern Africa, about the size of France, yet home to only around 2.6 million people, making it one of the least crowded nations on Earth. The Kalahari Desert's red and gray sands cover roughly 70 percent of the land. The capital, Gaborone, sits near the South African border in the southeast, where most people live. English is the official language, and Setswana is the national language spoken in nearly every home.

When Botswana became independent in 1966 it was one of the poorest countries in the world, with only a few kilometers of paved road. A year later diamonds were discovered, and careful management of that wealth built schools, clinics, and highways. Botswana has held peaceful elections ever since and is often called one of Africa's most stable democracies; it is a republic with a president elected by parliament. Wildlife tourism is the other pillar of the economy, drawing visitors to see the Okavango Delta and the largest elephant population anywhere.
landAndNature: Most of Botswana is flat Kalahari scrubland where grasses, thorny acacias, and camelthorn trees survive on little rain. In the northwest the Okavango River flows in from Angola and, instead of reaching the sea, fans out across the sand into a huge maze of channels, lagoons, and islands: the Okavango Delta, a UNESCO World Heritage Site alive with hippos, crocodiles, and lechwe antelope splashing through the shallows. Northeast of it lie the Makgadikgadi Pans, blinding white salt flats left by an ancient lake, where flamingos breed after rains and zebras migrate in tens of thousands. Chobe National Park holds vast herds of elephants; the country has about 130,000, more than any other. Lions, wild dogs, cheetahs, and meerkats also thrive.
peopleAndCulture: Most citizens are Tswana, organized in traditional communities where a kgotla, an open-air meeting under a tree, lets everyone speak before decisions are made. The San, or Basarwa, are the region's oldest inhabitants and speak languages full of click sounds. The word pula means rain, so precious here that it became the name of the currency and a cheer shouted at celebrations. Seswaa, slow-cooked pounded beef served with a stiff sorghum porridge, is the national dish, and mopane worms are a crunchy snack. Soccer is the most popular sport, and the country's runners have won Olympic medals; Letsile Tebogo took gold in the 200 meters at the 2024 Paris Games. Choral singing and the segaba, a one-stringed fiddle, are traditional arts.
history: The San have lived in the Kalahari for tens of thousands of years, leaving thousands of rock paintings at the Tsodilo Hills. Tswana-speaking farmers and cattle herders arrived over the following centuries and formed several chiefdoms. In 1885 Britain declared the area the Bechuanaland Protectorate, and in 1895 three chiefs, Khama III, Sebele I, and Bathoen I, traveled to London and persuaded the British not to hand their land to a mining company. Independence came on September 30, 1966, under the first president, Seretse Khama. Diamonds found at Orapa in 1967 transformed the economy. Botswana was hit hard by the HIV epidemic and became a leader in providing free treatment. In 2024 voters elected a new party to power for the first time since independence, and the handover was peaceful.
funFacts: Botswana's roughly 130,000 elephants outnumber those of any other country on Earth.
The Makgadikgadi salt pans are so large and flat that they can be seen clearly from space.
The blue on Botswana's flag stands for rain and water, and its black and white stripes stand for racial harmony, like a zebra's coat.
The Okavango is one of the very few large rivers in the world that never reaches the ocean.
The Jwaneng mine in Botswana is often described as the richest diamond mine in the world by value.
